cards.front: What did the Nuremberg Code establish?
cards.back: Drawn up in 1947 after unethical experiments on prisoners in Nazi camps during World War II, it established that research subjects must give informed consent and must be free to withdraw from an experiment at any time.

cards.front: What is the Declaration of Helsinki and why does it matter for trials?
cards.back: A statement of ethical principles for medical research on human subjects, issued by the World Medical Association in 1964 and regularly updated. It sets the widely accepted ground rules for human research and forms the ethical base of ICH-GCP: trials must be conducted according to its principles.

cards.front: What do the CIOMS guidelines add to the Declaration of Helsinki?
cards.back: The Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (guidelines first published 1993) gives detailed guidance on applying Helsinki to present-day research: HIV/AIDS research, post-study availability of treatment, women as subjects, confidentiality, compensation for adverse events and consent, while avoiding unnecessary suffering and weighing risk against benefit.

cards.front: Short note: Milestones that shaped research ethics and GCP

points: US Federal Food and Drugs Act: against adulterated or misbranded food and drugs
Sulphanilamide elixir tragedy: untested solvent (an antifreeze) killed over 100 people
Nuremberg Code after Nazi camp experiments: informed consent, right to withdraw
Promoted for morning sickness; babies born without limbs or with severe deformities
Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association): ethical base of ICH-GCP
Belmont Report (US National Commission, under the National Research Act 1974)
CIOMS guidelines applying Helsinki to modern research
ICH-GCP finalised 1996, effective 1997

cards.front: How do the Nuremberg Code and the Declaration of Helsinki differ in origin and standing?
cards.back: Nuremberg Code (1947) arose from the Nazi-camp experiments and laid down informed consent and the right to withdraw. Helsinki (1964, World Medical Association) is a regularly updated statement for research on human subjects and is the ethical base of ICH-GCP, so trials must follow it.

cards.front: How does GG14 use the Belmont Report's justice principle in the debate on foreign drug trials?
cards.back: The Belmont Report says research should not unduly involve groups unlikely to benefit from its later applications. Some ethicists argue that testing drugs abroad in populations who cannot afford the approved product breaches this principle. Defenders reply that such trials also bring medical care to underserved people.

cards.front: Essay: Evolution of ethics in clinical research

points: Rules grew out of harm: unsafe drugs and unethical experiments
1906 US Food and Drugs Act against adulterated or misbranded drugs
1937 sulphanilamide elixir deaths from an untested solvent
Thalidomide (marketed 1957, disaster 1962): limb deformities in babies
1947 Nuremberg Code: informed consent and right to withdraw
1964 Declaration of Helsinki (WMA), updated regularly
1979 Belmont Report
1993 CIOMS guidelines applying Helsinki to modern research
ICH-GCP finalised 1996, effective 1997, with Helsinki as its ethical base

cards.front: Complete: the four principles of medical ethics (Beauchamp and Childress)
cards.text: {{Autonomy}}: the person's right to make choices and hold views; {{beneficence}}: do good and contribute to welfare; {{non-maleficence}}: do no intentional harm; {{justice}}: treat everyone equally and share benefits fairly.

cards.front: What are the cardinal principle and the principle of precaution in research on human participants?
cards.back: The cardinal principle is respect for the dignity of persons. Precaution and risk minimisation require care at every stage so that participants and affected communities face minimum risk and no known irreversible harm. All guidelines demand both ethical and scientific review and informed consent.

cards.front: How do ICH-GCP and WHO-GCP differ?
cards.back: ICH-GCP was designed to harmonise technical requirements for drug registration across the US, Japan and EU and has 13 principles. WHO-GCP was written as a teaching tool for countries without their own guideline and has 14 principles (its principles 5 and 6 are combined in ICH-GCP). Both aim to promote good clinical practice.

cards.front: Short note: The 13 principles of ICH-GCP

points: Conduct per Declaration of Helsinki and regulations
Benefits must justify foreseeable risks
Subjects' rights, safety and well-being outweigh science and society
Freely given informed consent
Confidentiality of records
Adequate non-clinical and clinical data on the product
Scientifically sound, clear, detailed protocol
Prior IRB/IEC approval and protocol compliance
Medical decisions by a qualified physician or dentist
Staff qualified by education, training and experience
Records allow accurate reporting and verification
Investigational product made and stored per GMP and used per protocol
Quality systems for every aspect of the trial

cards.front: What are the Indian GCP guidelines and what is the principle of essentiality?
cards.back: CDSCO set up an expert committee that produced India's first GCP document in 2001, modelled on WHO, US FDA, ICH and EU guidelines. It lists 10 ethical principles in line with Helsinki, including informed consent, community agreement, non-exploitation, privacy and confidentiality, risk minimisation, and accountability and transparency of investigators and sponsors. Essentiality means human subjects should be used only when absolutely necessary and no alternative exists. The NDCT Rules 2019 define "GCP guidelines" as the CDSCO guidelines adopted by the Drugs Technical Advisory Board.

cards.front: What role do the ICMR ethical guidelines play in Indian research?
cards.back: ICMR issued Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research on Human Subjects in 2000, with planned periodic revision to keep researchers updated on bioethics. Ethics committees for biomedical and health research (as opposed to drug trials) are constituted under ICMR's National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants. Standard guidelines also make studies comparable across centres and help prevent duplicated research.

cards.front: Essay: Ethical framework for clinical research in India

points: Nuremberg Code, Helsinki, Belmont, CIOMS
Autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, justice
Respect for dignity; precaution; essentiality
ICH-GCP (13 principles); Indian GCP (CDSCO 2001); ICMR national ethical guidelines
NDCT Rules 2019 for drug trials
ICMR composition and quorum
Exempt, expedited and full review; periodic and continuing review
Decisions and record keeping
Informed consent; vulnerable groups
Placebo use and equipoise
Conflict of interest

cards.front: Short note: Informed consent in clinical research

points: Proper written informed consent must be obtained from the patient or trial subject before participation
Autonomy: freedom, dignity and confidentiality; right to join or leave the trial
Beneficence and non-maleficence
ICMR (2006) ethical guidelines for biomedical research on human participants (India)

cards.front: Complete: categories of ethics committee review by risk
cards.text: Proposals with less than minimal risk (e.g. research on educational practice) may be {{exempted}} from review; those with minimal risk (e.g. studies of already approved drugs or devices) get {{expedited}} review; those with more than minimal risk, or involving {{vulnerable}} groups such as children or psychiatric patients, need {{full}} committee review. The {{member secretary}} screens and categorises proposals.

cards.front: What kinds of ongoing review does an ethics committee carry out after approval?
cards.back: Periodic review of ongoing research at intervals of 6 months to 1 year; continuing review of any new information and adverse events; and interim review in special circumstances by a sub-committee, re-examined by the full committee as needed (e.g. quarterly).

cards.front: What decisions can an ethics committee reach, and how are records kept?
cards.back: Approval (only minor changes), approval with modifications, resubmission with more information, or outright disapproval. Decisions are preferably by consensus; invited subject experts give opinions but do not decide. Minutes are approved and signed by the chair, documents are confidential, and records are kept for 5 years after the trial ends.

cards.front: Short note: Composition of an ethics committee for biomedical and health research (ICMR)

points: Chairperson or vice-chairperson: respected, experienced, not affiliated with the institution
Member secretary: staff of the institution with research and ethics experience
Basic medical scientist
Clinician(s)
Legal expert (law degree)
Social scientist, philosopher, ethicist or theologian (may be from an NGO)
Lay person from the community
At least 5 members, medical and non-medical, technical and non-technical
At least one non-affiliated member; preferably the lay person
No decision valid without quorum
GCP or human-protection training (within 6 months of appointment)
Declare conflicts of interest; sign confidentiality agreement
Name, profession and affiliation made public

cards.front: Short note: What an ethics committee reviews in a proposal

points: Protocol; participant information sheet and consent form with translations
Investigator's brochure; PI's CV

Rationale and essentiality; specific objectives

Recruitment and inclusion/exclusion

Adequacy and clarity of information; contact persons
Justification for including those unable to consent
Conflicts of interest of investigator, institution and sponsor

cards.front: Short note: Role of a pharmacologist in an ethics committee

points: Pharmacologist is an integral member of institutional ethics committees
Clinical-trial protocols are reviewed only when at least five members are present, including a medical scientist (preferably a pharmacologist)
Ensures research protocols follow GCP guidelines
Assesses risk-benefit for participants and the community
Examines subject selection, inclusion and exclusion criteria
Safeguards rights, safety and well-being of all subjects, especially vulnerable ones
Gives an opinion on compensation after a serious adverse event
Every member needs training in GCP and regulatory requirements

cards.front: Short note: Institutional ethics committee

points: Every clinical trial must be scrutinised and approved by an independent ethics committee, as per GCP guidelines
Committee ensures the study does not breach autonomy, beneficence and non-maleficence
ICMR (2006) Ethical guidelines for biomedical research on human participants

cards.front: What is clinical equipoise and why does it matter ethically?
cards.back: Genuine uncertainty among experts about which treatment is better. It justifies randomising patients, because the trial is done precisely because doubt exists. Placebo-controlled trials are argued to violate equipoise and the principle of beneficence when a proven effective therapy is already available.

cards.front: What does the Declaration of Helsinki say about placebo controls?
cards.back: It discourages placebo controls when an alternative treatment is available, since patients randomised to placebo would in effect be denied treatment; every patient, including controls, should get the best proven methods and not suffer unnecessary pain. Where an available treatment prevents death or irreversible harm, a placebo control is generally inappropriate.

cards.front: What must the consent form of a placebo-controlled trial tell participants?
cards.back: What "placebo" means, in lay language; that they may receive it; why a placebo is used and what alternatives exist; how long they may be on placebo and the likely discomfort; the harm of not receiving or delaying effective treatment and that the condition may worsen; and that they may withdraw at any time.

cards.front: Short note: When is a placebo-controlled trial ethically justified?

points: No proven or approved therapy exists
Existing therapy is of doubtful or modest, inconsistent efficacy with frequent adverse effects, and the new drug is not expected to be better
Patients fully informed, autonomy kept, close monitoring, rescue treatment available, GCP followed
Existing therapy is highly and consistently effective: use an equivalence or non-inferiority design
Existing therapy prevents death or irreversible morbidity
Add-on design so all receive standard care
Minimal placebo exposure; early-escape and withdrawal rules
Smaller placebo arm; DSMB interim review

cards.front: When is it ethical to use a placebo in clinical practice?
cards.back: Only with the patient's welfare as the sole motive, to relieve suffering, when the condition has an unpredictable course, standard treatment fails or is not tolerated, or no effective therapy exists. It must never replace effective treatment, must be stopped if ineffective, and the doctor should answer honestly if asked about it; if it helps and nothing better exists, stopping it is unethical.

cards.front: Essay: Role of placebo in clinical trials and its ethical aspects

points: Placebo control; clinical equipoise means genuine expert doubt about which treatment is better
Violates equipoise and beneficence when proven effective therapy exists
Helsinki discourages placebo when an alternative treatment is available
No proven therapy exists
Existing therapy modest or inconsistent with frequent adverse effects, and new drug not expected to be better
Patients fully informed, monitored, rescue treatment available
Existing therapy highly effective: use equivalence or non-inferiority design
Therapy prevents death or irreversible harm
Add-on design, minimal exposure, early escape, smaller placebo arm, DSMB review
Consent explains placebo, alternatives, duration, harm of delayed treatment and right to withdraw

cards.front: What is a conflict of interest in research, and how should a reader handle it?
cards.back: A situation where personal factors (e.g. funding or financial gain) could influence professional judgement or responsibilities. Such conflicts are common; what matters is whether they were recognised and managed. When appraising a paper, check the declared funding source and any statement on how a conflict was handled. Ethics committee members must also declare conflicts.

cards.front: How does ICD-11 define burnout, and what are its three dimensions?
cards.back: A syndrome from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed, marked by (1) exhaustion or energy depletion, (2) mental distance from the job, negativism or cynicism, and (3) reduced professional efficacy.

cards.front: Who described the standard features of burnout, and what is the traffic-light model for?
cards.back: Christina Maslach and colleagues described the standard features in the 1970s. The traffic-light model gives a stepwise, colour-coded way to recognise and assess medical burnout: stop and recognise, pause and find causes, then start coping and treatment.

cards.front: Short note: Burnout in doctors: causes, consequences and prevention

points: Workload: long hours, night duty, administrative tasks, patient overload
Poor teamwork and relationships; lack of reward, autonomy and job security
Work-family conflict; lack of resources and development opportunities
More major medical errors and adverse patient incidents
Lower patient satisfaction; doctors leave practice
Depression and coronary risk linked to effort-reward imbalance
"Traffic-light" model: stop and recognise, pause and find causes, then start coping and treatment
Flexible schedules
Mindfulness-based stress reduction, meditation
System-level changes in addition to individual measures

cards.front: Why must burnout prevention in doctors include system-level changes and not only individual help?
cards.back: Main causes are workplace factors (long hours, night duty, administrative load, poor teamwork, lack of reward, autonomy, resources). Individual measures such as mindfulness help, but cannot remove these causes, so system changes (e.g. flexible schedules) are needed as well. Untreated burnout raises medical errors and makes doctors leave practice.

cards.front: A resident on repeated night duty shows exhaustion, cynicism and a medication error. Analyse using burnout concepts.
cards.back: These are the ICD-11 dimensions of burnout (exhaustion, mental distance or cynicism, reduced efficacy), and the error is the consequence the text links to burnout. Use the traffic-light steps: recognise, find causes (night duty, workload, poor support), then start coping measures. Prevention needs system change such as flexible schedules, with mindfulness as a supplement.

cards.front: What is the pharmacologist's role in medical education?
cards.back: Teaching undergraduates (pharmacology is a second-year MBBS and BDS subject), postgraduates (including thesis guidance), and nursing and pharmacy students. Content includes rational drug use and essential drugs, drug classes, effects, toxicity, ADRs and interactions, telling real drug information from promotional claims, dose calculation by age, sex and health status, and correct routes. Pharmacologists also educate practising doctors on rational use, new drugs, ADR reporting, drug audit and generic prescribing.

cards.front: Which two WHO rational-use interventions relate to medical education?
cards.back: Problem-based pharmacotherapy training in undergraduate curricula, and continuing in-service medical education made a requirement for licensure.

cards.front: Besides guiding treatment, procurement and reimbursement, what else does Sarkar say an essential medicines list identifies?
cards.back: The 'must know' drugs for the teaching and training of health care professionals.

cards.front: What is AETCOM?
cards.back: A longitudinal programme, set out in a 2018 booklet, that helps students build competence in the attitude, ethics and communication domains.

cards.front: How many AETCOM learning modules are there in each professional year, and how many hours does each year take?
cards.back: Professional year I: 5 modules, 34 hours. Year II: 8 modules, 37 hours. Year III: 5 modules, 25 hours. Year IV: 9 modules, 44 hours.

cards.front: How often must MD Pharmacology PG teaching sessions be held?

cards.front: What is the place of laboratory work in MD Pharmacology PG learning?

cards.front: What is a drug and therapeutics committee (DTC)?
cards.back: A body set up in districts and hospitals to promote rational drug use, one of the WHO key interventions. A hospital pharmacologist may act as its convener.

cards.front: What does a DTC formulate for a hospital?
cards.back: Policies for prescribing, storing and safely dispensing drugs, a hospital formulary, and hospital antibiotic policy (with the clinical microbiologist and the head of critical care). Purpose: rational and safe use of medicines.

cards.front: What is pharmacovigilance?
cards.back: The science and activities of detecting, assessing, understanding and preventing adverse drug effects or other drug-related problems (WHO definition). Its aim is to make drugs safer by monitoring adverse reactions.

cards.front: What is a signal in pharmacovigilance?
cards.back: Reported information on a possible causal link between a drug and an adverse event whose link was unknown or incompletely documented before. Early detection lets regulators act on it.

cards.front: How is causality of an adverse drug event judged?
cards.back: By temporal relation to the drug, previous knowledge of the reaction, dechallenge (it settles when the drug stops) and rechallenge (it returns on re-exposure, often unethical to test). Graded definite, probable, possible or doubtful. It separates drug-caused events from events caused by the disease.

cards.front: Which scales do pharmacovigilance centres use to score ADR causality and severity?
cards.back: The Naranjo algorithm for causality and the modified Hartwig scale for severity grading.

cards.front: Why can spontaneous reporting not give the true incidence of an ADR?
cards.back: The numerator (affected patients) and denominator (patients exposed) are unknown, and underreporting is substantial, so reports only flag possible signals.

cards.front: What is the FDA Sentinel System?
cards.back: A partnership of the FDA with many organisations that uses curated electronic health data for observational pharmacoepidemiologic studies of possible safety signals.

cards.front: Short note: Methods of signal detection in pharmacovigilance

points: Spontaneous (voluntary) reports, e.g. UK Yellow Card and Indian ADR forms
Prescription-event monitoring and case reports in the literature
Relevance: new drug (4 years from approval), unknown reaction, serious reaction
Identify duplicate reports using sex, age or date of birth, and exposure dates
Causality assessment must validate the link before a case counts
Controlled observational studies, e.g. pharmacoepidemiology and the Sentinel System
Post-marketing trials, used sparingly because of ethical limits
Case reports suffice for rare events close in time to exposure, with a large excess risk
Signals go to the regulator (CDSCO and the national PvPI in India)
Action: label change, restriction or withdrawal

Full membership is not defined in the owner books; state it from the institution's own rules
Hospital formulary: pharmacologist facilitates its formulation
Policies for prescribing, storage and safe dispensing
Prescription audits and drug utilisation studies
Narcotic and psychotropic drugs
Chemotherapeutic agents and radioactive drugs
Hospital antibiotic policy with the clinical microbiologist and head of critical care
Adverse drug event reporting, management and monitoring
Medication error detection and mitigation
Pharmacologist keeps watch on ADRs and drug-drug interactions

cards.front: Essay: Ethics committee: constitution, review and responsibilities

points: Independent body of medical, non-medical, scientific and non-scientific members
Protects the rights, safety and well-being of trial subjects
At least five members present, including a medical scientist (preferably a pharmacologist) and a clinician
Legal expert, social scientist or NGO representative, and a lay person preferred
At least one non-affiliated member; no decision valid without quorum
Scientific evaluation before ethical review
Categories by risk: expedited, full, or exempt

cards.front: Elixir sulfanilamide disaster: which solvent caused the deaths, and what did US law change?
cards.back: Diethylene glycol, an antifreeze, was used as the solvent, and more than 100 children died. The 1938 amendment to the US Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act then required toxicity studies and approval of a New Drug Application before marketing, but still did not require proof of efficacy.

cards.front: What did the Harris-Kefauver amendments of 1962 require?
cards.back: Passed after the thalidomide disaster. Proof of efficacy as well as documentation of relative safety by risk-to-benefit assessment before approval. They also introduced informed consent of trial participants, gave the FDA authority over prescription-drug advertising, and introduced good manufacturing practice standards.

cards.front: Thalidomide: original use, trade name and the defect it caused
cards.back: A hypnotic marketed in West Germany in 1957 as Contergan and used for morning sickness in pregnancy. Early intrauterine exposure caused phocomelia, with malformed or absent limbs.

cards.front: What did the US FDA Amendments Act of 2007 add for drug safety?
cards.back: It let the FDA require risk evaluation and mitigation strategies (REMS) and postapproval studies, and set up a population-based surveillance system. REMS is one of three regulatory tools for changing prescribing behaviour, with communication and withdrawal.

cards.front: Tuskegee syphilis study: who was studied, for how long, and why does it matter?
cards.back: The US Public Health Service ran the Tuskegee syphilis study in Black men from 1932 to 1972. It is described as the most infamous example of medical experimentation in Black communities and left a lasting legacy of mistrust of health care and research.

cards.front: Define good clinical practice (GCP).
cards.back: An international ethical and scientific quality standard for designing, conducting, monitoring, auditing, recording, analysing and reporting clinical trials in human participants, ensuring their rights, safety and confidentiality and the credibility of trial data.

cards.front: Which five parties does Katzung list as the stakeholders in GCP?
cards.back: The sponsor, investigator, study participant, regulatory authority and ethics committee.

cards.front: Short note: Katzung list of seven principles of good clinical practice

points: Conduct must follow the Declaration of Helsinki and be consistent with GCP
Rights, safety and well-being of participants come first
Participation voluntary and based on an informed consent process
Protocol reviewed by an IRB or independent ethics committee
Based on current scientific knowledge and done by qualified individuals
Protocol concise, feasible and able to give consistent results
Roles and responsibilities defined and documented
Quality control, with investigational products made, stored, shipped and handled to specification

cards.front: What does an IRB or IEC decide about a research proposal, and on what grounds?
cards.back: It may approve, require modification of, or disapprove the research after judging that risks are minimised, risks are reasonable against benefit and scientific gain, subject selection is equitable, consent is effective, and vulnerable groups are safeguarded.

cards.front: What membership does an IRB or IEC require?
cards.back: At least five members of varied background, including at least one with primary expertise in a scientific area, one in a non-scientific area, and one not affiliated with the institution. Many also include clergy, social workers and attorneys. This lets the board judge protocols against law, professional standards and community attitudes.

cards.front: Short note: Contents of a clinical research protocol

points: Title page with candidate, degree, supervisor, department and institution
Investigators and their roles
Introduction and review of literature
Rationale, aim, hypotheses and objectives
Study design, population and subjects, sample size and statistical power
Data collection methods, data management and statistical analysis
Project management, personnel, duration and follow-up
Budget, strengths and limitations
Ethical considerations and consent process
Patient information sheet, case record form and informed consent form

cards.front: Short note: What an informed consent form must tell a trial participant

points: Purpose of the study
Trial treatments and randomisation
Trial procedures and experimental aspects
Risks of the study
Benefits of the procedures
Alternative treatments, if available
Compensation or treatment for injury during the study
Any payment required during the study
Subject's responsibilities
Confidentiality of the participant
New information likely to be gained
Voluntary participation and contact persons
Rights if study-related injury occurs
Reasons for termination, total duration and total number of subjects

cards.front: How is an informed consent form signed and witnessed?
cards.back: It records the study title, the subject initials and identifiers, consent statements initialled by the volunteer, the subject signature or thumb impression, the legally acceptable representative, the investigator signature and name, and the witness signature and name.

cards.front: What does an investigator undertake in the investigator undertaking?
cards.back: A legal commitment to conduct the trial under GCP and the approval conditions. Not to begin before ethics committee and DCGI approval, to adhere to the protocol under personal supervision, to ensure ethics review, to report unexpected serious adverse events to the sponsor within 24 hours and to the ethics committee within 7 days, and to maintain records for audit.

cards.front: What is an academic clinical trial under the NDCT Rules 2019?
cards.back: A trial of a drug already approved for a claim, started by an investigator or academic or research institution for a new indication, route, dose or dosage form, whose results are intended only for academic or research use and not for marketing approval.

cards.front: How do the NDCT Rules 2019 define a serious adverse event?
cards.back: An untoward medical occurrence during a trial causing death, permanent disability, hospitalisation or prolongation of hospitalisation, persistent or significant disability, congenital anomaly or birth defect, or a life-threatening event.

cards.front: Under the NDCT Rules 2019, what affiliations must the chairperson and member secretary of a trial ethics committee have?
cards.back: The chairperson must be a member not affiliated with the institute, while the member secretary must be a member affiliated with the institute.

cards.front: What qualifications and training does the NDCT Rules 2019 require of ethics committee members?
cards.back: Medical scientist and clinician members must have a postgraduate qualification, adequate experience and clarity of role. Every member must complete training specified by the Central Licensing Authority, and an untrained member ceases to hold office.

cards.front: How does a trial ethics committee handle a member's conflict of interest under the NDCT Rules 2019?
cards.back: No member with a conflict may take part in oversight of that protocol. All members sign a declaration, a conflicted member may withdraw in writing, and the conflict is recorded in the minutes.

cards.front: Short note: Functions of a trial ethics committee under the NDCT Rules 2019

points: Review and approve the protocol and related documents
Oversee conduct to protect the rights, safety and well-being of trial subjects
Review at appropriate intervals using progress reports, monitoring or audit reports, or site visits
Record in writing the reasons for rejection or for requiring a protocol change, with a copy to the Central Licensing Authority
Keep records for five years after completion
Analyse serious adverse event documents and forward its report to the Central Licensing Authority
Order discontinuation or suspension if rights, safety or well-being are compromised
Allow authorised officers to inspect premises, records and documents

cards.front: What happens if the Central Licensing Authority does not respond to an ethics committee registration application within 45 working days?
cards.back: The registration is deemed granted and legally valid, and the applicant must inform the Authority in Form CT-02A before starting the committee functions. A rejection can be appealed within 60 working days.

cards.front: How long is registration of an ethics committee for biomedical and health research valid?
cards.back: Provisional registration is valid for two years. Final registration in Form CT-03 is valid for five years, and renewal is applied for at least 90 days before expiry.

cards.front: How did the old Schedule Y ethics committee composition differ from ICH-GCP?
cards.back: Schedule Y required at least seven members, while ICH-GCP required at least five including one non-scientific member. Indian GCP recommended a fairly small committee of 5 to 7 members, with 12 to 15 as the maximum.

cards.front: Short note: Placebo and nocebo

points: An inert substance given as if it were a medicine
Acts by psychodynamic rather than pharmacodynamic means and can produce responses similar to an active drug
Suggestible people who respond readily are called placebo reactors
The effect depends largely on the physician-patient relationship
Can release endorphins and produce analgesia, which naloxone blocks
Used as a dummy control in trials and sometimes when no active drug is needed
The converse: a negative psychodynamic effect from pessimism or loss of faith in the drug or physician
It can oppose the therapeutic effect of active medication
Placebo effects are highly variable even in the same person
It therefore has a very limited role in practical therapeutics

cards.front: Why is uncertainty about comparative safety not the same as clinical equipoise?
cards.back: In a postmarketing comparison of two marketed drugs, entering the trial when one may carry a serious adverse effect means accepting increased risk with no expectation of added benefit. True equipoise requires genuine uncertainty about which treatment is better.

cards.front: How do the NDCT Rules 2019 define post-trial access?
cards.back: Making a new or investigational drug available to a trial subject after the trial, when the drug was found beneficial to that subject, for the period considered necessary by the investigator and ethics committee.

cards.front: What three principles does the Charter on Medical Professionalism set out?
cards.back: The primacy of patient welfare, patient autonomy, and social justice.

cards.front: Short note: Qualities of a humane physician

points: Being available and expressing sincere concern
Taking time to explain all aspects of the illness
Dealing without judgement when culture, lifestyle, attitudes or values differ
Monitoring one own strong positive or negative reactions
Keeping the patient best interest as the motive
Appreciating what each patient values most
Learnt through deliberate, unhurried and repeated conversation

cards.front: What must a physician discuss for informed consent in clinical care?
cards.back: The alternatives for care, and the risks, benefits and likely consequences of each. The physician must ensure the patient understands, encourage questions, and have no real or apparent conflict of interest.

cards.front: What are the steps of shared decision-making?
cards.back: Inform and educate the patient, discuss the nature, risks, benefits and alternatives of care and their consequences, answer questions, check understanding, make a recommendation, and help the patient deliberate.

cards.front: Define moral distress and name its consequences.
cards.back: Distress when ethically appropriate action is hindered by institutional policy or culture, hierarchy, limited resources or other constraints. It can cause anger, anxiety, depression, frustration, fatigue, work dissatisfaction and burnout.

cards.front: What is a just culture in response to medical errors?
cards.back: A system that encourages open, honest reporting of errors as essential to learning and shifts focus from individual blame to system design. Professional discipline is still used for gross incompetence, recklessness, impairment or boundary violations.

cards.front: How should conflicts of interest be managed?
cards.back: Recognise them, disclose them, discuss with the chief of service, and manage or recuse as appropriate. Not all conflicts are financial, since conflicts of commitment can also arise.

cards.front: What rules now apply to gifts from pharmaceutical companies to physicians?
cards.back: Accepting gifts from drug companies is forbidden at many academic medical centres and by law in several US states. The federal Open Payments website lists payments and amounts given to named physicians.

cards.front: What are the five goals of MD Pharmacology training?
cards.back: Acquisition of knowledge, acquisition of skills, teaching and training, research, and professionalism, ethics and communication skills.

cards.front: Short note: Theory papers in the MD Pharmacology examination

points: Basic sciences as applied to pharmacology
Systemic pharmacology
Clinical pharmacology, experimentation, research, biostatistics and education
Recent advances in pharmacology

cards.front: How is the MD Pharmacology practical examination organised?
cards.back: It is spread over two days and focuses mainly on the psychomotor domain, with long exercises, short exercises, 10 to 15 OSPE stations, and assessment of teaching or presentation skills.

cards.front: What are the prerequisites for appearing in the MD Pharmacology summative examination?
cards.back: Submission of a log book of training, rotation postings, departmental presentations and internal assessment reports; at least two presentations at a national conference; and one research paper published or accepted in an indexed journal.

cards.front: What is the recommended quarterly assessment schedule during MD Pharmacology training?
cards.back: Case presentation once a week; laboratory performance twice a week; journal club once a week; seminar once a fortnight; case discussions once a fortnight or month; and an interdepartmental case or seminar once a month.

cards.front: Short note: Mandatory psychomotor competencies of an MD Pharmacology student

points: Write rational prescriptions and analyse prescriptions
Predict, report and assess causality of adverse drug reactions
Use organ bath, analgesiometer, physiograph, convulsiometer and similar equipment
Prepare drug solutions and determine EC50, ED50, pD2 and pA2
Design a trial protocol
Prepare and administer the participant information sheet and informed consent form
Evaluate promotional literature and prepare a package insert
Calculate and interpret pharmacokinetic parameters
Critically appraise a paper and present in class and at academic meetings
Prepare material for teaching-learning and assessment
